"Without a body, without physical evidence, some of these cases simply stall," said a former district attorney not connected to the case. "When a defendant offers to lead you to remains, prosecutors have to weigh the value of that information against what they may have to give up in a plea deal."

Search teams, working off Kimball's directions, have combed through rural stretches of Colorado in recent search operations, using cadaver dogs, ground-penetrating radar and forensic anthropologists to comb through fields, wooded areas and other remote terrain. Officials say the process has been painstaking, as years of weather and environmental exposure have complicated recovery efforts.

Families of the missing have expressed a mixture of relief and anguish at the development.

"We've waited so long just to know," said a relative of one victim, who asked not to be named. "It doesn't bring them back, but at least now we can finally lay them to rest."

The Colorado Bureau of Investigation and local sheriff's departments involved in the case have declined to comment extensively, citing the ongoing nature of the investigation. Kimball's criminal history includes prior convictions for fraud and other offenses, but investigators say evidence gathered in recent years pointed to his involvement in a series of disappearances that many had assumed would never be solved.

For now, authorities say their focus remains on recovering and identifying remains, notifying next of kin, and building the strongest possible case against Kimball for any additional charges that may follow.
